patterns: how many forms does a verb have
entries.answer: A verb carries the action, the state or the description, and every English sentence needs at least one. Verbs change form to agree with the subject and with the time, so one word appears as runs, running and ran, and that three-way system is what makes the language work. They also connect, which is what be, have and do are for, and a sentence built only from a noun and a verb still needs a subject and usually a helper.

patterns: when to use to plus verb
entries.answer: The infinitive is the plain form of a verb, the one a dictionary prints, and English uses it after a modal, after to, and in a handful of other fixed positions. Its two jobs are turning a noun into an action, as in I want to leave, and making a whole clause behave as a noun, as in I forgot to call. The position it cannot take is the subject, which is why a clause cannot open with a bare infinitive and has to use the -ing form instead.

patterns: is the ing form always a gerund
entries.answer: A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun, so reading is relaxing and I enjoy reading, while the identical -ing form used descriptively, as in the running water, is doing a different job. The test is whether the word names an activity or describes a thing, and what would replace it settles it. The common error is confusing the two, so swimming is fun names an activity while the swimming is fun describes water.

patterns: difference between will not and cannot
entries.answer: A modal verb carries mood and permission rather than action, and English modals never change form for person or tense, which is what makes them both easy and unusual. The core set is can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must and ought. The most important fact about them is the negative, because could not and cannot differ sharply, and the second means impossible rather than merely declined.

entries.answer: A transitive verb needs an object to complete its meaning, as in she wrote a letter, and an intransitive one does not, as in she wrote. Many common verbs manage both without changing form, so he ran a company means something quite different from he ran. The quick test is to ask what, and an answer that follows means the verb is transitive, which is the fastest way to classify an unfamiliar one.

entries.answer: An intransitive verb is complete on its own and refuses an object, so the mistake is supplying one and saying he arrived to the office. Verbs of movement, state and change are usually intransitive, covering arrive, sit, sleep, laugh, rise and happen. Some change meaning when an object appears, since the boat floated and the boat floated the harbour are entirely different claims, and that is a real ambiguity rather than a rule.

entries.answer: An auxiliary is a helping verb that carries tense, negation and question formation while the main verb supplies the meaning, so in she is working the word is does the tense. They come in three kinds, primary for tense as in has seen, modal for mood, and a small set that appears only in questions and negatives, which are do, does and did. That last group is the one learners miss, because affirmative sentences never show it.
